claims.text: A defect-aware multiscale model integrating ab initio electronic structure, phonon scattering, oxygen-defect physics, and machine-learning calibration can improve conductivity predictions for bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Oxygen-related defects produce additional electron-scattering effects in HfNbTaTiZr.
Accounting for oxygen-related defects will improve prediction accuracy in both the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes relative to ideal-crystal analytical predictions.
Density functional theory and molecular dynamics can quantify defect and phonon scattering for use in the proposed conductivity model.
A machine-learning regression model calibrated against conductivity measurements from oxygen-containing samples can improve the multiscale model.
Quantum and defect-scattering corrections are significant in the 0–200 K regime.
Phonon scattering dominates electrical transport in the 300–1200 K regime.
Oxygen impurities create defect sites in bulk HfNbTaTiZr.
Oxygen-induced defect sites alter electron-scattering rates.
Oxygen-induced defect sites change the electronic density of states.
Oxygen-induced defect sites change charge-carrier mean free paths.
Combining oxygen-induced defect scattering with phonon-electron interactions will capture the real electronic transport behavior more accurately.
Machine-learning calibration of ambiguous parameters against experimental benchmarks will improve agreement with measured conductivity trends.
The proposed model will predict measured conductivity within ±10% throughout both specified temperature regimes.
Existing analytical models can deviate from measurements by 20–50%.
The asserted 20–50% errors of existing analytical models arise from neglecting defect scattering and oxygen impurity effects.
Perfect-crystal analytical predictions typically incur substantial errors for oxygen-containing HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed model is applicable only to bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen and to the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K intervals.
Additional mechanisms or model refinement may be required outside the specified composition and temperature limits.

contradictions.description: The falsification rule treats an error greater than 10% as disproving improvement over existing models, but a result above 10% could still outperform the claimed 20–50% errors of those models. It directly falsifies the ±10% accuracy target, not necessarily the comparative-improvement claim.

The model is to be calibrated against experimental conductivity data, while the proposed benchmark does not explicitly require independent held-out samples or temperatures. Consequently, the evaluation data could overlap the calibration data despite the request for a held-out benchmark.
